name: Sentence fragments: missing the subject
scope: The most common fragment shape and how to spot it. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'Ran all the way home from the bus stop.' A complete sentence needs a SUBJECT (who did it) and a VERB (what they did). This has a verb but no subject; the fix is 'She ran all the way home from the bus stop.' T2: define SENTENCE FRAGMENT in-context -- a group of words that looks like a sentence (starts with a capital, ends with a period) but is missing a subject or verb, so it cannot stand alone. T3: identify-the-fragment task -- given four groups of words, three are complete sentences and one is a subject-less fragment ('Barked at the mail carrier through the fence.'); the answer names the fragment. T4: the participle-phrase trap that looks like a sentence -- 'Sitting quietly under the maple tree.' has a verb-looking word (SITTING) but no real verb and no subject; the fix adds both: 'The cat was sitting quietly under the maple tree.' T5: fix-the-fragment judgment -- given a fragment and four proposed fixes, pick the fix that adds the missing element without adding a new error (comma splice, tense mismatch, or run-on).
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.213 (sentence fragments); Strunk and White 'The Elements of Style' rule 4 (a sentence must contain a subject and a verb). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Sentence clause structure' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the subject-verb-required rule. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the participle-vs-verb distinction in Chicago 5.113.
framing_note: Punchline via misuse: the fragment sounds off because the reader waits for a subject that never comes. Vocab-teaching invariant: T2 defines SENTENCE FRAGMENT inline. Everyday apolitical scenes (pets, running for the bus, backyard trees). Distractor pool: run-ons, comma splices, dangling modifiers, complete-but-short sentences that a kid might over-diagnose as fragments. CHOICE PARITY: if answer is a corrected sentence, all four choices are similar-length rewrites.

name: Sentence fragments: missing the verb
scope: The verbless fragment. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'The huge orange cat on the windowsill.' The reader waits for what the cat did -- and gets nothing. The fix adds a verb: 'The huge orange cat SAT on the windowsill.' T2: name the pattern -- a NOUN PHRASE standing alone is a fragment because it has a subject but no VERB (the action word) to tell you what happened. T3: identify-the-fragment task -- given four items, three are complete and one is a verbless noun-pile ('My grandmother's amazing chocolate chip cookies with walnuts.'); pick the fragment. T4: the prepositional-phrase pile that fools the eye -- 'In the corner of the garage behind the old bicycles under a blue tarp.' Reads like a sentence but is all setting and no action; fix: 'We found the missing puzzle in the corner of the garage.' T5: fix-the-fragment judgment across four candidate rewrites -- pick the one that supplies the verb correctly, not one that instead makes the noun phrase a subordinate clause dangling from the previous sentence.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.213 (fragments); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'sentence fragment'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Sentence clause structure' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the noun-phrase-alone case.
framing_note: Punchline via the trailing-off pile-up (reader hangs waiting for the verb). Vocab-teaching at T2 for NOUN PHRASE. Apolitical family/kitchen/garage examples. Distractor pool: subject-missing fragments, run-ons, comma splices.

name: Sentence fragments: subordinate clause stranded
scope: The dependent-clause fragment. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'Because it was raining.' has a subject (IT) and a verb (WAS RAINING) but starts with BECAUSE, a subordinating conjunction, which makes the whole clause DEPENDENT -- it needs a main clause to complete the thought. Fix: 'We stayed inside because it was raining.' T2: define SUBORDINATING CONJUNCTION in-context and list the common ones -- because, although, since, when, while, if, until, after, before, unless. Any sentence that starts with one and has no matching main clause is a fragment. T3: identify-the-fragment task -- four items each start with a subordinator; three attach to a main clause, one stands alone. T4: the intentional-fragment exception -- fiction writers use fragments deliberately for punch ('Silence. Then a knock at the door.'); punctuation and register signal INTENT vs mistake, but in formal writing all fragments read as bugs. T5: fix-the-fragment judgment -- given a stranded subordinate clause, pick the fix that either attaches it to the previous sentence with proper punctuation or rewrites it to remove the subordinator.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.230 (subordinating conjunctions); Strunk and White rule 4. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Dependent clause' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the subordinator list and dependent-clause definition.
framing_note: Punchline via the mid-thought BECAUSE that leaves the reader hanging. Vocab-teaching at T2 for SUBORDINATING CONJUNCTION. Apolitical everyday scenes (weather, staying in, kids at play). Distractor pool: run-ons, verbless fragments, subject-less fragments. T4 addresses the stylistic-fragment nuance without confusing kids about the base rule.

name: Run-on sentences (fused sentences): no punctuation at all
scope: The fused-sentence bug. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'I love pizza it's my favorite food.' Two complete sentences ('I love pizza' and 'It's my favorite food') are jammed together with no punctuation between them; this is called a RUN-ON or FUSED sentence. T2: name the four fixes -- (a) a PERIOD between them ('I love pizza. It's my favorite food.'), (b) a SEMICOLON between them ('I love pizza; it's my favorite food.'), (c) a COMMA plus a coordinating conjunction ('I love pizza, and it's my favorite food.'), or (d) turning one clause into a subordinate clause ('I love pizza because it's my favorite food.'). T3: define INDEPENDENT CLAUSE in-context -- a group of words with a subject and verb that could stand alone as a sentence. Two independent clauses fused without punctuation = run-on. T4: identify-the-run-on task -- given four items, three are correctly punctuated and one is fused; pick the fused one. T5: pick-the-best-fix judgment -- given a fused sentence and four candidate fixes, pick the one that best fits the meaning (not just any grammatical fix -- sometimes the semicolon is right, sometimes the subordinator is right).
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 6.62 (run-on sentences); Strunk and White rule 5. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Run-on sentence' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the fused-sentence definition and the four canonical fixes.
framing_note: Punchline via the two-clauses-crashing-together speed of the wrong version. Vocab-teaching at T3 for INDEPENDENT CLAUSE. Apolitical food/hobby examples. Distractor pool: comma splices, fragments, correctly punctuated compound sentences. Distinct from comma splices (which have a comma between the clauses) -- that distinction is its own ladder.

name: Comma splices: two sentences joined ONLY by a comma
scope: The comma-splice sibling of the run-on. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'I love pizza, it's my favorite food.' The comma is TOO WEAK to join two complete sentences on its own; this is called a COMMA SPLICE. T2: the four fixes are the same as for run-ons -- period, semicolon, add a coordinating conjunction after the comma (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so), or subordinate one clause. T3: identify-the-comma-splice task -- distinguish a comma splice ('The rain stopped, the game continued.') from a correctly punctuated compound sentence ('The rain stopped, and the game continued.') and from a fused run-on ('The rain stopped the game continued.'). T4: the accepted stylistic exception -- SHORT parallel clauses in journalism and fiction can be spliced ('I came, I saw, I conquered.' -- Julius Caesar, 47 BC); the rule bends when the effect is deliberate and the clauses are tight. T5: run-on vs comma-splice vs correct-compound distinction across four candidates -- pick the ONLY comma splice.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 6.62 (comma splices); Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'comma splice'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Comma splice' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the Caesar tricolon and the accepted-in-fiction nuance. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: 'Veni, vidi, vici' attributed to Julius Caesar reporting his victory at Zela in 47 BC (Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar).
framing_note: Punchline via the weak-comma that fails to hold the two clauses. FANBOYS mnemonic appears here as a fix, not the main topic. Vocab-teaching implicit from the run-on ladder (INDEPENDENT CLAUSE). Apolitical + historical (Caesar quote as neutral rhetorical anchor). Distractor pool: run-ons, correctly punctuated compounds, fragments.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Caesar's military campaigns; here 'Veni, vidi, vici' is a punctuation exemplar, not a history lesson.

name: FANBOYS: the seven coordinating conjunctions
scope: The T1 mnemonic that unlocks compound sentences. T1: FANBOYS stands for the seven COORDINATING CONJUNCTIONS in English -- For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So. These are the words that can join two independent clauses with a comma. T2: define COORDINATING CONJUNCTION in-context -- a word that joins two grammatically equal elements (two nouns, two verbs, two independent clauses) without making one depend on the other. T3: identify-the-FANBOYS-use task -- given four sentences, pick the one that correctly uses a FANBOYS word with a comma to join two independent clauses ('The bell rang, AND the students filed out.') vs one that misuses it. T4: the no-comma-needed exception -- when a FANBOYS word joins two verbs sharing one subject, no comma is needed ('The dog ran and jumped.'); the comma appears only when there are two separate independent clauses. T5: distinguish coordinating (FANBOYS) from SUBORDINATING conjunctions (because, although, since, when, while, if) -- coordinators join equals; subordinators make one clause depend on the other. Given four sentences, pick the one that uses a subordinator masquerading in a coordinator's role.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.201 (coordinating conjunctions) and 6.28 (comma with coordinating conjunctions). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Conjunction (grammar)' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the FANBOYS mnemonic and the coordinating/subordinating distinction.
framing_note: Snappy T1 mnemonic anchoring the whole strand. Vocab-teaching at T2 for COORDINATING CONJUNCTION. Punchline via the FANBOYS acronym itself (a kid remembers it). Apolitical everyday examples (bells, dogs, kids). Distractor pool: subordinating conjunctions, conjunctive adverbs (however, therefore).

name: Independent vs dependent clauses: the standalone test
scope: The clause classification that everything else rests on. T1: define CLAUSE in-context -- a group of words with a subject and a verb. There are two kinds: INDEPENDENT (can stand alone as a sentence) and DEPENDENT (cannot stand alone, needs a main clause). T2: the standalone test -- if you can put a period at the end and it makes sense on its own, it's independent. 'The dog barked.' is independent. 'When the dog barked' is dependent -- the WHEN makes it wait for what happened next. T3: identify-the-type task -- given four clauses, pick which are independent and which are dependent. T4: the SUBORDINATOR-list rule -- clauses that begin with because, although, since, when, while, if, until, after, before, unless, or a RELATIVE PRONOUN (who, which, that) are dependent. T5: analyze a complex sentence -- given 'Although the storm knocked out the power, we still finished dinner by candlelight', identify the dependent clause and the independent clause and explain which subordinator makes the first one dependent.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition sections 5.220-5.231 (clauses). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Dependent clause' and 'Independent clause' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the standalone-test framing and the subordinator/relative-pronoun list.
framing_note: Foundational vocab ladder. Vocab-teaching at T1-T2 for CLAUSE, INDEPENDENT, DEPENDENT. Apolitical everyday examples (dogs, storms, dinner). Distractor pool: phrases mistaken for clauses (no verb, so not a clause at all), fragments.

name: Sentence types: simple, compound, complex, compound-complex
scope: The four-way classification. T1: a SIMPLE sentence has one independent clause ('The cat slept.'). T2: a COMPOUND sentence has two independent clauses joined by a FANBOYS conjunction ('The cat slept, AND the dog snored.'). T3: a COMPLEX sentence has one independent and one or more dependent clauses ('While the cat slept, the dog snored.' -- WHILE makes the first clause dependent). T4: a COMPOUND-COMPLEX sentence has two or more independent clauses AND at least one dependent clause ('While the cat slept, the dog snored, AND the goldfish swam in circles.'). T5: identify-the-type task -- given four sentences, classify each and pick the compound-complex one, distinguishing it from a plain compound (no dependent clause) and a plain complex (only one independent clause).
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.213 (sentence types). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Sentence clause structure' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the four-way classification and canonical examples.
framing_note: Vocab-teaching ladder for the four types, each with a quoted example. Apolitical pet examples throughout for continuity. Distractor pool: mis-classifications (compound called complex, complex called compound-complex). Not a punchline ladder per se -- but the vocab is essential.

name: Parallel structure in lists: same grammatical form
scope: The parallel-list rule. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'I like swimming, hiking, and to run.' The first two are GERUNDS (-ing forms) and the third is an INFINITIVE (to + verb); the mix reads bumpy. The fix is 'I like swimming, hiking, and running' OR 'I like to swim, to hike, and to run' -- but pick one form and stick with it. T2: define PARALLEL STRUCTURE in-context -- items in a list should share the same grammatical form (all gerunds, or all infinitives, or all nouns, or all clauses). T3: identify-the-non-parallel task -- given four sentences, three have parallel lists and one breaks the pattern; pick the broken one. T4: fix-the-parallelism task -- given a broken list, pick the rewrite that makes all items match ('The recipe called for eggs, flour, and to add sugar' fixed to 'eggs, flour, and sugar' or 'to add eggs, to add flour, and to add sugar'). T5: analyze a longer sentence -- 'The coach wants players who arrive on time, follow the plays, and to give effort' has a three-item list where the third breaks the who-verb pattern; identify the break and pick the correct rewrite.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.242 (parallel structure); Strunk and White rule 15 (express coordinate ideas in similar form). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Parallelism (grammar)' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the gerund/infinitive/noun mismatch cases.
framing_note: Punchline via the bumpy read of the third item breaking the pattern. Vocab-teaching at T2 for PARALLEL STRUCTURE. Apolitical hobby/recipe/sports examples. Distractor pool: other list errors (comma placement, missing Oxford comma), fragments, run-ons.

name: Parallel structure with correlative conjunctions (both/and, either/or, not only/but also)
scope: The paired-conjunction parallelism rule. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'She not only sings BUT also DANCING.' The word after NOT ONLY is a verb (SINGS); the word after BUT ALSO should be a matching verb, not a gerund. Fix: 'She not only SINGS but also DANCES.' T2: define CORRELATIVE CONJUNCTION in-context -- a pair of words that work together to join equal elements: both/and, either/or, neither/nor, not only/but also, whether/or. Whatever comes after the first word must match in form what comes after the second. T3: identify-the-mismatch task -- given four sentences using correlatives, three are parallel and one mismatches the two halves; pick the mismatch. T4: fix-the-correlative task -- 'Either you finish your homework or going to bed early' fixed to 'Either you finish your homework or you go to bed early'. T5: subtler-mismatch judgment -- 'The trip was both exhausting AND a lot of fun' pairs an adjective (EXHAUSTING) with a noun phrase (A LOT OF FUN); the fix is 'both exhausting AND fun' or 'both an exhausting trip AND a fun one'. Meaning stays, form matches.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.244 (correlative conjunctions); Strunk and White rule 15. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Correlative conjunction' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the standard pairs list and the parallelism-required rule.
framing_note: Punchline via the mismatch across the paired conjunctions. Vocab-teaching at T2 for CORRELATIVE CONJUNCTION. Apolitical school/family scenes. Distractor pool: simple list parallelism errors, non-parallel comparisons.

name: Garden-path sentences: the horse raced past the barn fell
scope: The canonical parsing-ambiguity ladder. T1: the canonical example -- 'The horse raced past the barn fell.' Reads as broken until you realize RACED PAST THE BARN is a REDUCED RELATIVE CLAUSE meaning 'that was raced past the barn'; the main verb of the whole sentence is FELL. The horse that was raced past the barn fell. T2: define GARDEN-PATH SENTENCE in-context -- a sentence that leads the reader down one interpretation and then forces them to BACKTRACK when a later word doesn't fit. Named for 'leading someone up the garden path' (deceiving). Cited by Thomas Bever in a 1970 paper as a classic example of temporary syntactic ambiguity. T3: another canonical case -- 'The old man the boat.' Reads as fragment until you realize THE OLD is the subject (elderly people as a group) and MAN is the VERB (to man the boat = to staff it). Fix nothing -- it's correct. T4: a third canonical case -- 'The complex houses married and single soldiers and their families.' COMPLEX is a noun (a housing complex), HOUSES is a verb (contains); once you see it, the sentence parses. T5: identify-the-garden-path task -- given four sentences, three parse smoothly on first read and one requires backtracking; pick the garden-path one and explain the reparsing.
source: PRIMARY: Thomas G. Bever, 'The Cognitive Basis for Linguistic Structures' (1970) -- source of the 'horse raced past the barn fell' example. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Garden-path sentence' (browser, 2026-09-05) for Bever 1970 attribution and the three canonical examples (horse/barn, old/man/boat, complex/houses). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: Bever's paper appeared in Hayes ed. 'Cognition and the Development of Language' (Wiley 1970); reduced-relative-clause is the standard linguistic term for the horse/barn construction.
framing_note: Punchline via the backtrack-realization -- kid re-reads and hears the sentence click into place. Vocab-teaching at T2 for GARDEN-PATH SENTENCE. Bever 1970 is a linguistic-history anchor without violating the grade-10 ceiling (he's cited as the person who popularized the example, not as jargon-source). Distractor pool: fragments, run-ons, actually-broken sentences. Distinctly a T3-T5 topic (harder than the T1 average).

name: Misplaced modifiers: I saw the boy with the telescope
scope: The classic word-order ambiguity. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'I saw the boy with the telescope.' Who has the telescope, the SEER or the BOY? The modifier WITH THE TELESCOPE sits next to BOY, so grammar says the boy has it -- but everyone reads it both ways, and that ambiguity is the bug. T2: define MISPLACED MODIFIER in-context -- a word or phrase that describes something but is placed so far from what it describes that the sentence becomes unclear or absurd. Fix: move it closer to what it modifies. T3: fix-the-modifier task -- 'I nearly drove my kids to school every day for a year' vs 'I drove my kids to school nearly every day for a year' -- NEARLY modifies DROVE in the first (you almost drove them!) and EVERY DAY in the second (most days). T4: the classic ONLY problem -- 'I only ate two cookies' vs 'I ate only two cookies' -- ONLY placement changes meaning. Similarly JUST, ALMOST, EVEN. T5: identify-the-misplaced-modifier task -- given four sentences, three are clear and one is misplaced ('The waiter served the customers on paper plates' -- were the customers on the plates?); pick the misplaced one and rewrite it.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.171 (misplaced modifiers); Strunk and White rule 20 (keep related words together). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Misplaced modifier' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the telescope example and the ONLY/NEARLY/JUST placement rules.
framing_note: Punchline via the double-reading -- kid laughs at the customers-on-plates image. Vocab-teaching at T2 for MISPLACED MODIFIER. Apolitical everyday scenes (kids, cookies, waiters). Distractor pool: dangling modifiers, squinting modifiers, parallel-structure errors.

name: Dangling modifiers: walking down the street, the trees were beautiful
scope: The subject-less introductory modifier bug. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'Walking down the street, the trees were beautiful.' The modifier WALKING DOWN THE STREET has no clear subject in the sentence, so grammar attaches it to the nearest noun (THE TREES), meaning the trees were walking. The fix names the walker: 'Walking down the street, I noticed how beautiful the trees were.' T2: define DANGLING MODIFIER in-context -- an introductory phrase that describes an action but the doer of that action is missing from the main clause, so the phrase dangles and gets stuck to the wrong noun. T3: another classic -- 'Having finished my homework, the TV was turned on.' The TV finished the homework? Fix: 'Having finished my homework, I turned on the TV.' T4: fix-the-dangler task -- given four rewrites, pick the one that supplies the missing doer as the subject of the main clause (not one that just moves words around without fixing the dangle). T5: distinguish DANGLING from MISPLACED modifiers -- a MISPLACED modifier attaches to the wrong noun that IS in the sentence; a DANGLING modifier's doer is entirely MISSING. Given four sentences, pick the ONLY dangler.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.115 (dangling participles) and 5.171. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Dangling modifier' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the walking-trees canonical example and the doer-missing definition.
framing_note: Punchline via the trees-walking absurdity. Vocab-teaching at T2 for DANGLING MODIFIER. Apolitical everyday scenes (walking, homework, TV). Distractor pool: misplaced modifiers, squinting modifiers, non-parallel constructions.

name: Squinting modifiers: the adverb that faces both ways
scope: The subtlest of the three modifier bugs. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'The teacher told the class often to study.' Does OFTEN modify TOLD (the teacher told them often) or TO STUDY (told them to study often)? The adverb SQUINTS -- it looks both ways. T2: define SQUINTING MODIFIER in-context -- an adverb placed between two verbs so that it could modify either the one before it or the one after. Fix: move the adverb next to whichever verb it should modify. T3: fix-the-squinter task -- 'Students who study rarely fail the test' (do they rarely study, or rarely fail?) fixed to 'Students who rarely study fail the test' OR 'Students who study rarely fail the test' with a comma. T4: another case -- 'The people who exercise regularly stay healthy' -- REGULARLY squints between EXERCISE and STAY. T5: distinguish SQUINTING from MISPLACED and DANGLING modifiers -- squinting is when the modifier could attach to either of TWO candidates that are both in the sentence; misplaced is when it's clearly attached to the wrong one; dangling is when the doer is missing entirely. Given four sentences, pick the ONLY squinter.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.171 (squinting modifiers); Fowler's Modern English Usage entry 'squinting adverbs'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Squinting modifier' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the two-way-facing definition and the OFTEN/RARELY/REGULARLY canonical positions.
framing_note: Punchline via the both-directions ambiguity. Vocab-teaching at T2 for SQUINTING MODIFIER. Apolitical classroom/exercise/study scenes. Distractor pool: misplaced modifiers, dangling modifiers, parallel errors. T5 explicitly compares all three modifier bugs -- rewards the kid who worked through the whole modifier sub-strand.

name: Zombie rule: never split an infinitive
scope: The debunking of the split-infinitive superstition. T1: the canonical example -- 'to boldly go where no man has gone before' (the opening narration of Star Trek, 1966) puts BOLDLY between TO and GO, splitting the infinitive. The old prescriptive rule said never do this; the modern rule says it's fine. T2: define SPLIT INFINITIVE in-context -- putting an adverb (like BOLDLY, QUICKLY, CAREFULLY) between the TO and the VERB of an infinitive. Where did the rule come from? A 19th-century belief that English should imitate Latin, where infinitives are ONE word (amare = 'to love') and can't be split. English infinitives are two words and CAN be split. T3: when it's fine (most of the time) -- 'She promised to CAREFULLY consider the offer' reads more clearly than 'She promised carefully to consider' (squinting!) or 'She promised to consider carefully' (fine but different rhythm). T4: when to still avoid it -- only when the split creates awkwardness or ambiguity ('to more than double the budget' is standard; 'to boldly, without hesitation, and with great enthusiasm go' is bad because it's a HUGE gap). T5: identify-the-zombie-rule task -- given four 'rules', pick which one is a genuine standard rule and which are zombie superstitions (never split infinitives, never end with a preposition, never begin with AND).
source: PRIMARY: Fowler's Modern English Usage (1st edition 1926) entry 'split infinitive' -- famously debunked the superstition; Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'split infinitive'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Split infinitive' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the Latin-model origin of the ban and the Star Trek 'to boldly go' example (from the opening narration of the original series, 1966). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: Star Trek opening narration 'to boldly go where no man has gone before' first aired 8 September 1966; Fowler's 1926 debunking is the standard citation.
framing_note: Vision-mandated: this rung invokes the prescriptive-vs-descriptive controversy explicitly (see grammar.json framing STANCE). Punchline via the fake-rule reveal -- kid learns a 'rule' their teacher may still enforce is actually a myth. Vocab-teaching at T2 for SPLIT INFINITIVE. Star Trek + Fowler as neutral pop-culture and reference anchors. Distractor pool: other zombie rules (ending with prepositions, starting with AND), real rules that are similar (agreement of split verb phrases).

name: Zombie rule: never end a sentence with a preposition
scope: The other big prescriptive zombie. T1: the canonical debunker -- 'This is the sort of English up with which I will not put' is apocryphally attributed to Winston Churchill mocking the never-end-with-a-preposition rule; the natural 'This is the sort of English I will not put up with' is fine. T2: define PREPOSITION in-context -- a word showing relationship (on, in, at, with, by, to, from, for, of, about, over, under). English routinely ends sentences with prepositions when the alternative is stilted ('What are you looking AT?' vs the stilted 'At what are you looking?'). T3: where the rule came from -- 17th-century poet John Dryden decided in the 1670s that ending with a preposition was ugly, again by analogy to Latin. Modern style guides (Fowler, Chicago, Merriam-Webster) all say it's fine. T4: when to reword anyway -- long formal writing or ceremonial prose may sound better without the terminal preposition ('the friend to whom I wrote' vs 'the friend I wrote to' -- both fine, register differs). T5: identify the ONE zombie rule among four candidates. Note: the Churchill quote is APOCRYPHAL -- there is no documented source; it appears attributed to him only in an unsigned 1942 magazine article and became famous after his death.
source: PRIMARY: Fowler's Modern English Usage (1926) entry 'preposition at end'; Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'preposition at end'; John Dryden's 'Defence of the Epilogue' (1672) as the origin of the ban. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Preposition stranding' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the Dryden 1672 origin, the Fowler debunking, and the Churchill quote's apocryphal status (first appears in a 1942 unsigned Strand Magazine article, not in any Churchill speech or writing). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: attribute the Churchill quote as 'apocryphally attributed to Churchill' -- do NOT present as a real quote.
framing_note: Vision-mandated: prescriptive-vs-descriptive stance. Punchline via the deliberately-clunky 'up with which I will not put' -- the fake rule makes English sound insane. Vocab-teaching at T2 for PREPOSITION. Accuracy rail: Churchill quote must be attributed as apocryphal (bank's accuracy rail is explicit). Distractor pool: other zombie rules, real preposition rules (redundant prepositions, wrong prepositions).
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Churchill as a political figure; here he's a grammar-anecdote source (apocryphal).

name: Zombie rule: never begin a sentence with And or But
scope: The third major prescriptive zombie. T1: the canonical debunker -- opening sentences with AND or BUT is fine and has been done by great writers for centuries. 'And God said, Let there be light' (Genesis 1:3, King James Bible 1611) -- a sentence starting with AND in the second verse of the most-read book in English. T2: name the myth -- a school-teacher tradition (not any real style guide) that coordinating conjunctions can't start sentences, because they 'join two things' and there's nothing before them. Reality: the joined thing is the previous sentence, and sentence-initial AND or BUT creates a pointed rhythm. T3: modern style-guide verdict -- Fowler's Modern English Usage, the Chicago Manual of Style, Merriam-Webster, and the Associated Press Stylebook all explicitly say beginning a sentence with a conjunction is acceptable. Chicago (17th ed, section 5.203) notes about 10% of sentences in professional writing begin with AND, BUT, SO, or YET. T4: when to overuse it -- if EVERY sentence starts with BUT, the rhythm dies; use sentence-initial conjunctions for emphasis, not as a default connector. T5: identify the zombie -- given four claimed grammar rules, pick the one that is a real rule (subject-verb agreement, no comma splice, parallel structure in lists) and reject the sentence-initial-conjunction myth.
source: PRIMARY: Fowler's Modern English Usage entry 'and (to begin a sentence with)'; Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.203; Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage entry 'and: at the beginning of a sentence'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Coordinating conjunction' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the myth's schoolteacher origin and the Chicago 10% statistic. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: 'And God said, Let there be light' is Genesis 1:3 in the KJV (1611).
framing_note: Vision-mandated: prescriptive-vs-descriptive stance. Punchline via the KJV opening as a canonical AND-start. Vocab-teaching at T2 (leans on FANBOYS ladder). Neutral religious-text citation (Genesis 1:3 is used as a WRITING example, not a theological one -- 'the most-read book in English' is descriptive fact). Distractor pool: other zombie rules, real rules.
history_overlap: THEOLOGY owns Genesis as story; here the verse is a grammar exemplar of a well-known sentence starting with AND.

name: Passive voice: when it hides the actor
scope: The passive-voice judgment ladder. T1: the canonical hidden-actor punchline -- 'Mistakes were made.' By whom? The passive-voice construction lets the writer NAME the mistake without naming the maker. The active version -- 'I made mistakes' -- is more honest. T2: define PASSIVE VOICE in-context -- a sentence structure where the SUBJECT receives the action instead of doing it ('The ball was thrown by Tom' is passive; 'Tom threw the ball' is active). Formed with a form of TO BE + past participle. T3: passive is NOT wrong per se -- it's the right choice when the actor is unknown ('My bike was stolen'), obvious ('The suspect was arrested'), or unimportant to the point ('Water is boiled at 100 degrees Celsius'). Scientific writing uses passive routinely to focus on the process. T4: when active is clearly better -- when the ACTOR matters, name them. 'The vase was broken' hides who; 'The cat knocked the vase off the shelf' tells the story. T5: identify the ONE sentence among four where passive is masking responsibility that should be assigned (e.g., 'Errors were discovered in the report' vs 'The auditor found errors in the report').
source: PRIMARY: Strunk and White 'The Elements of Style' rule 14 (use the active voice); Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.115 (passive voice); Steven Pinker 'The Sense of Style' (2014) chapter 4 for the modern nuanced view. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Passive voice' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the 'mistakes were made' example and the legitimate uses (unknown actor, scientific writing). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: 'Mistakes were made' famously used by Nixon-era press secretaries and later politicians; frame as an example of agent-hiding, not politically.
framing_note: Vision-mandated: this is the ACTIVE-VOICE = RESPONSIBILITY rule from feedback_active_voice_responsibility.md, load-bearing bank-wide. Punchline via the hidden actor. Vocab-teaching at T2 for PASSIVE VOICE. Apolitical everyday examples (broken vases, stolen bikes, scientific processes). The 'mistakes were made' quote is used as a NEUTRAL agent-hiding example, not attributed to any specific politician. Distractor pool: sentences with correct passive use (unknown actor), sentences with awkward active constructions.

name: Nominalizations: zombie nouns that hide the verb
scope: The Helen-Sword ladder. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'We will make a decision about the schedule.' The verb DECIDE is hiding inside the noun DECISION. The concise version is 'We will decide about the schedule.' T2: define NOMINALIZATION in-context -- turning a strong verb into a weak noun ('decide' -> 'decision', 'analyze' -> 'analysis', 'implement' -> 'implementation', 'utilize' -> 'utilization'). Helen Sword's 2012 New York Times essay 'Zombie Nouns' called these nouns 'zombies' because they eat the life out of your writing. T3: nominalization-fix task -- 'The committee held a discussion about the proposal' -> 'The committee discussed the proposal'. 'The team gave consideration to the plan' -> 'The team considered the plan'. Each fix drops words AND makes the actor more active. T4: the -TION/-MENT/-ANCE giveaway -- most nominalizations end in these suffixes. Not every -tion word is a nominalization (NATION isn't hiding a verb); but if you see MANY -tion words in a sentence, look for verbs to un-hide. T5: rewrite a longer passage -- given a bureaucratic sentence with three nominalizations, produce a rewrite that uses active verbs and cuts the word count.
source: PRIMARY: Helen Sword, 'Zombie Nouns' (New York Times opinion essay, 23 July 2012); Steven Pinker 'The Sense of Style' (2014) chapter 2. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Nominalization' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the -tion/-ment/-ance pattern and the Helen Sword essay attribution. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: Sword's essay is titled 'Zombie Nouns' and appeared in the NYT Opinionator blog on 23 July 2012; confirm date.
framing_note: Punchline via the un-hiding of the verb -- kid sees a bloated sentence collapse to a tight one. Vocab-teaching at T2 for NOMINALIZATION. Sword 2012 is a modern reference-anchor (not jargon-source). Apolitical committee/team/office examples. Distractor pool: passive-voice examples, wordy-but-not-nominalized sentences, unnecessary hedges.

name: Wordy vs concise: cut the deadweight
scope: The tight-writing rewrite ladder. T1: the canonical WRONG-VERSION -- 'At this point in time, we should begin the meeting.' Five words (AT THIS POINT IN TIME) doing the work of one (NOW). The concise version is 'Let's begin the meeting now.' T2: the common cuts -- 'due to the fact that' -> BECAUSE; 'in the event that' -> IF; 'in order to' -> TO; 'a large number of' -> MANY; 'at the present time' -> NOW; 'in spite of the fact that' -> ALTHOUGH. Strunk and White's rule 17: 'Omit needless words.' T3: fix-the-wordy task -- given four rewrites of a bloated sentence, pick the one that cuts deadweight without dropping meaning. T4: redundancy patterns -- 'past history' (history is always past), 'true fact' (facts are true by definition), 'end result' (results are end states), 'basic fundamentals' (fundamentals are basic), 'each and every' (pick one). T5: rewrite a passage -- given a paragraph with three common wordiness patterns, produce the tight version and cut at least a third of the words.
source: PRIMARY: Strunk and White 'The Elements of Style' rule 17 (omit needless words); William Zinsser 'On Writing Well' (1976) chapter 2 (Clutter). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Elements of Style' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the Strunk 1918 / Strunk-White 1959 dates and the 'omit needless words' rule. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: Strunk's 'The Elements of Style' first published 1918 as a private printing at Cornell; the E.B. White revision that made it famous appeared 1959.
framing_note: Punchline via the deflation of the pompous phrase. Vocab-teaching implicit (uses categories from earlier). Strunk-White as a canonical writing-manual reference. Apolitical everyday-writing examples (meetings, homework, emails). Distractor pool: nominalizations (its own ladder), passive voice, redundant modifiers.

name: Coordination vs subordination: two ways to combine ideas
scope: The two-tool ladder for joining clauses. T1: two ways to join 'The rain stopped' and 'The game continued'. COORDINATION treats them as equals: 'The rain stopped, AND the game continued.' SUBORDINATION makes one dependent on the other: 'When the rain stopped, the game continued.' Both are grammatically correct; the choice depends on which idea you want to emphasize. T2: define COORDINATION and SUBORDINATION in-context -- coordination uses FANBOYS (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) to join equal clauses; subordination uses subordinating conjunctions (because, although, when, if, since, while) to attach a dependent clause to a main clause. T3: choose-the-emphasis task -- given two facts and a question about which to emphasize, pick the coordination version if they're equally important OR the subordination version if one supports the other. T4: the run-on / comma-splice avoidance -- if you have two independent clauses jammed together, you can fix them by COORDINATING (comma + FANBOYS) or SUBORDINATING (turning one into a dependent clause with a subordinator). Both are legitimate fixes. T5: identify-the-technique task -- given four rewrites of the same fused-sentence bug, distinguish the coordinated fixes from the subordinated fixes and pick the one that best fits a specified emphasis.
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition sections 5.201 (coordination) and 5.230 (subordination); Strunk and White rule 18. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Coordination (linguistics)' and 'Subordination (linguistics)' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the equal-vs-dependent distinction.
framing_note: Vocab-teaching at T2. Ties the FANBOYS ladder to the subordinator ladder. Apolitical everyday examples. Distractor pool: fragments, run-ons, comma splices -- all as WRONG options a coordination or subordination fix would correct.

name: Intentional fragments: when writers break the rule on purpose
scope: The stylistic-fragment nuance. T1: the canonical example -- 'It was cold. Very cold. Bitter, biting, teeth-chattering cold.' The last two 'sentences' are FRAGMENTS -- they have no verbs -- but they hammer the point home. Fiction writers, journalists, and speechwriters use fragments deliberately for punch. T2: the rule for INTENTIONAL vs UNINTENTIONAL fragments -- intentional fragments are short, punchy, and clearly deliberate; they follow a complete sentence that establishes context. Unintentional fragments look like the writer forgot to finish the thought. T3: identify-the-intentional task -- given four fragments, three read as bugs (dropped verbs, orphaned subordinate clauses) and one reads as clearly intentional (short, punchy, follows a complete sentence). T4: register matters -- fragments are common in fiction, journalism, and advertising; RARE in academic writing, legal writing, or scientific reports. A grade-10 essay for English class should use fragments SPARINGLY; a report for science class should use NONE. T5: fix-or-keep judgment -- given four fragments in different contexts, pick which should be fixed (essay, report) and which can stay (dialogue, punchline, opening hook).
source: PRIMARY: Chicago Manual of Style 17th edition section 5.213 (sentence fragments, note on stylistic use); William Zinsser 'On Writing Well' chapter 6 (short sentences). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Sentence clause structure' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the intentional-fragment convention in fiction and journalism.
framing_note: The intentional-fragment ladder guards against the kid over-diagnosing every fragment as a bug (fixing 'Very cold.' would kill the writing). Punchline via the punchy prose the fragment enables. Vocab-teaching implicit (leans on fragment ladders). Register awareness at T4 is a grade-10 skill. Distractor pool: unintentional fragments (real bugs), correctly punctuated short sentences with verbs.
